To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the Indians of the Bolivian highlands were not pre-political, but that they were politically active and that they were interested in the national project.

the indigenous population of Bolivia, far from being pre-political, alien and passive, took an active part in the national project and that the national discourse had an important effect on the indigenous response to it.
the Indians were active political subjects, that the national project was an important factor for them in their political actions and that the Indians were interested in the national project.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the way in which a group that was not part of the national project became part of it, in the process of which they also became politicised.
the political and cultural processes that led to the creation of a new social actor, the Indian citizen.
the process of the politicisation of the indigenous people of Bolivia, and the way in which they became part of the national project.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
, from a political perspective, the Indians were neither passive nor pre-political.
the indigenous population was not a pre-political entity but a political one.
the Indians were active and political actors who were not only able to adapt to the new political context of the country, but who also managed to impose their own interests on it.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
, in the case of Bolivia, the indigenous rebellions of the nineteenth century were a consequence of the political process of the nation-state.
the Indians, far from being pre-political, were active participants in the political process.

the indigenous population was not a pre-political, pre-modern, pre-national, passive and incomprehensible entity, but rather that it was the result of a process of politicisation and nationalisation that took place between 1826 and the 1920s.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the indigenous population did not simply react to the national discourse but rather appropriated it, adapting it to their own purposes.
the Indians’ political apprenticeship was a result of their own actions.
the Indians were not only a political subject but were also a subject of politics.
